prompt: A measured vibration–rotation spectrum, such as that of HCl, does not show the equal line spacing that the rigid rotor–harmonic oscillator model predicts. Which two effects does the section say are responsible?

choices.text: Vibration–rotation coupling and centrifugal distortion
Nuclear spin coupling and electron spin coupling
choices.why: Spins play no part in this section. The spacings change because B̃ depends on v (vibration–rotation coupling) and because the bond stretches as the molecule rotates (centrifugal distortion).

choices.text: Overtone bands and the missing Q branch
choices.why: Overtones are separate bands near twice ν̃, and the missing Q branch only leaves a gap at the band center. The spacings change because of vibration–rotation coupling and centrifugal distortion.

choices.text: Collisions between gas molecules and the Doppler effect
choices.why: Those widen lines; they don't move them steadily closer together or farther apart. The section names vibration–rotation coupling and centrifugal distortion.

explanation: R-branch lines crowd together and P-branch lines spread apart because of two effects: rotational–vibrational coupling, in which B̃ depends on v, and centrifugal distortion, in which the bond stretches as the molecule rotates.

prompt: In the measured HCl vibration–rotation spectrum, what happens to the spacing between neighboring R-branch lines as J increases?

choices.text: It gets smaller; the lines crowd together
It gets larger; the lines spread apart
choices.why: That is what the P-branch lines do. Toward higher energy, the R-branch lines move closer together.

choices.text: It stays at exactly 2B̃ for every pair of lines
choices.why: Equal spacing of 2B̃ is what the simple model predicts. In the real spectrum the R-branch spacing shrinks as J increases.

choices.text: It alternates between large and small gaps
choices.why: The spacing changes smoothly, not back and forth: it shrinks steadily as J increases.

explanation: As the energy increases, the R-branch lines become more and more similar in energy, so they move closer together. P-branch lines do the opposite and spread apart toward lower energy.

prompt: Spectra are not always plotted with the P branch on the left. Which branch can you recognize by its lines spreading farther apart as the wavenumber decreases?

choices.text: The P branch
The R branch
choices.why: R-branch lines do the opposite: they crowd closer together as the wavenumber increases.

choices.text: The Q branch
choices.why: Diatomic molecules such as HCl show no Q branch. The lines that spread apart toward lower wavenumber are the P branch.

choices.text: The overtone band
choices.why: An overtone is a separate band near twice the fundamental wavenumber. Within the fundamental band, the lines that spread apart toward lower wavenumber are the P branch.

explanation: The section says the branches can be labeled by their spacing: P-branch lines get farther apart as the wavenumber decreases, while R-branch lines get closer together as the wavenumber increases.

prompt: The HCl vibration–rotation band appears as a series of discrete peaks rather than one smooth band. What do the discrete peaks indicate?

choices.text: The molecule's angular momentum is quantized
The bond length of HCl never changes
choices.why: Bond lengths do change with v. The separate peaks show that the rotational angular momentum can take only certain values.

choices.text: HCl has only one rotational level
choices.why: One level couldn't give a whole series of peaks. Each peak starts from a different J, because the angular momentum is quantized.

choices.text: The sample contains a mixture of many molecules
choices.why: The sample is HCl. The separate peaks are transitions between its quantized rotational levels.

explanation: The discrete peaks indicate a quantization of the molecule's angular momentum: each line starts from a different rotational level J. Lines on one side of the center go with a decrease in angular momentum, those on the other side with an increase.

prompt: The measured HCl absorption spectrum discussed in this section belongs to which vibrational transition?

choices.why: At room temperature nearly all molecules start in v = 0. The band discussed is the fundamental, v = 0 → 1.
That would be an overtone, at about twice the wavenumber. The spectrum discussed is v = 0 → 1.
That would be emission. The spectrum is an absorption spectrum from v = 0 to v = 1.

explanation: The section's HCl spectrum is an absorption spectrum from the v = 0 to the v = 1 vibrational level. All of its P-branch and R-branch lines belong to this one vibrational transition.

prompt: In the rotational constant B̃ = h/(8π^2cμR_e^2), what does R_e stand for?

choices.text: The bond length
The square of the bond length
choices.why: R_e is the bond length itself. Its square, R_e^2, is what appears in the denominator.

choices.text: The radius of the heavier atom
choices.why: R_e is the distance between the two nuclei, the bond length, not the size of one atom.

choices.text: The reduced mass of the molecule
choices.why: The reduced mass is μ, a separate symbol in the formula. R_e is the bond length.

explanation: R_e is the bond length, and B̃ depends on its square inversely: B̃ ∝ 1/R_e^2. A longer bond gives a smaller rotational constant.

prompt: How does the average bond length of a diatomic molecule change as the vibrational quantum number v increases?

choices.text: It increases
It decreases
choices.why: Higher levels vibrate with larger amplitude, and the bond can stretch out much more than it can squeeze in, so the average length grows.

choices.text: It stays fixed at R_e
choices.why: R_e, at the bottom of the potential well, doesn't change, but the average bond length over the vibration grows with v.

choices.text: It grows in direct proportion to v
choices.why: It grows, but not in proportion to v: that would make the bond length zero at v = 0.

explanation: The average bond length increases with v. Higher vibrational states have larger amplitudes, and on a real, anharmonic potential the bond can stretch out much more than it can squeeze in.

prompt: On a harmonic-oscillator potential curve, a level's vibrational amplitude can be pictured as the distance from one side of the parabola to the other at that level's energy. How does this distance change as v increases?

choices.text: It gets larger
It gets smaller
choices.why: Higher levels sit higher in the parabola, where it is wider, so the amplitude grows.

choices.text: It stays the same for every level
choices.why: The parabola widens as the energy rises, so higher levels have larger amplitudes.

choices.text: It shrinks to zero at high v
choices.why: A wider parabola at higher energy means a larger amplitude, not a vanishing one.

explanation: Higher vibrational states lie higher in the potential well, where it is wider, so they have larger amplitudes: the bond stretches and squeezes over a greater range.

prompt: A larger vibrational amplitude makes the average bond longer on a real, anharmonic potential, but hardly at all on a harmonic one. Why?

choices.text: The bond can stretch out much more than it squeezes in
The bond can squeeze in much more than it stretches out
choices.why: That would shorten the average bond. A real potential is steep on the short side and gentle on the long side, so the bond stretches more.

choices.text: The reduced mass grows as v increases
choices.why: The masses don't change with v. The average length grows because the anharmonic well lets the bond stretch out far.

choices.text: The bond stops vibrating at high v
choices.why: The vibration doesn't stop; it gets bigger. On an anharmonic well that bigger vibration stretches the bond out more than it squeezes it in.

explanation: On a harmonic parabola, a bigger vibration stretches and squeezes the bond by about the same amount. A real, anharmonic potential lets the bond stretch out greatly while it can squeeze in only a little, so the average bond length grows with v.

prompt: The average bond length grows with v. What happens to R_e, the bond length at the minimum of the potential energy curve?

choices.text: It stays the same for every v
It grows along with v
choices.why: R_e marks the bottom of the potential well, which doesn't move. Only the vibrationally averaged bond length grows with v.

choices.text: It shrinks as v increases
choices.why: R_e is fixed by the shape of the potential, not by v. The average bond length, not R_e, changes with v.

choices.text: It is directly proportional to v
choices.why: R_e doesn't depend on v at all; it is fixed at the minimum of the potential.

explanation: R_e is fixed at the potential minimum. What grows with v is the vibrationally averaged bond length, and that is why the rotational constant changes from one vibrational level to the next.

prompt: Why is the rotational constant B̃_1 of the v = 1 level smaller than B̃_0 of the v = 0 level?

choices.text: The average bond is longer in v = 1
The average bond is shorter in v = 1
choices.why: A shorter bond would give a larger B̃. The bond is longer on average in v = 1, and B̃ ∝ 1/R^2.

choices.text: The reduced mass is larger in v = 1
choices.why: The reduced mass depends only on the masses of the atoms, which don't change. B̃ falls because the average bond is longer.

choices.text: The molecule rotates faster in v = 1
choices.why: B̃ is a property of the level, set by the masses and the bond length. It falls because the average bond is longer in v = 1.

explanation: B̃ ∝ 1/R^2, and the average bond length is larger in v = 1 than in v = 0, so B̃_1 < B̃_0.

prompt: According to B̃_v = B̃_e − α̃_e(v + 1/2), how does B̃_v change each time v goes up by one?

choices.text: It falls by α̃_e
It falls by α̃_e/2
choices.why: (v + 1/2) goes up by a whole 1 each time v does, so B̃_v falls by α̃_e. The 1/2 only affects the starting value, B̃_0.

choices.text: It rises by α̃_e
choices.why: The minus sign means B̃_v gets smaller as v grows, because the bond gets longer on average.

choices.text: It is divided by v
choices.why: B̃_v falls in a straight line with v, by the same step α̃_e each time; it does not go as 1/v.

explanation: B̃_v decreases linearly with v. From v to v + 1, (v + 1/2) increases by 1, so B̃_v drops by α̃_e; for example, B̃_0 − B̃_1 = α̃_e.

prompt: What does the section call the dependence of the rotational constant B̃ on the vibrational state v?

choices.text: The vibration–rotation interaction
Centrifugal distortion
choices.why: Centrifugal distortion is the bond stretching as the molecule rotates faster, at higher J. The dependence of B̃ on v is the vibration–rotation interaction.

choices.text: The Franck–Condon principle
choices.why: That principle is about electronic transitions. B̃ depending on v is the vibration–rotation interaction.

choices.text: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation
choices.why: That approximation separates electronic from nuclear motion. B̃ depending on v is called the vibration–rotation interaction.

explanation: The rotational constant that depends on the vibrational state is written B̃_v, and the dependence of B̃ on v is called the vibration–rotation interaction.

prompt: The rigid rotor–harmonic oscillator energy is Ẽ_(v, J) = ν̃(v + 1/2) + B̃J(J + 1). What change does the section make to include the vibration–rotation interaction?

choices.text: B̃ is replaced by B̃_v, which depends on v
ν̃ is replaced by a value that depends on J
choices.why: The vibrational part stays ν̃(v + 1/2). It is the rotational constant that becomes B̃_v.

choices.text: A term in J^2(J + 1)^2 is added
choices.why: A term like that describes centrifugal distortion, the subject of Section 13.4. Here B̃ is simply replaced by B̃_v.

choices.text: (v + 1/2) is replaced by v
choices.why: The vibrational energy keeps its (v + 1/2). The change is that the rotational constant becomes B̃_v.

explanation: Writing Ẽ_(v, J) = ν̃(v + 1/2) + B̃_v J(J + 1) gives each vibrational level its own rotational constant. Since B̃_1 < B̃_0, the rotational levels of v = 1 are slightly closer together than those of v = 0.

prompt: The rotational constant depends on v as B̃_v = B̃_e − α̃_e(v + 1/2). For HCl, take B̃_e = 10.59 cm^−1 and α̃_e = 0.30 cm^−1. What is B̃_1, the rotational constant of the v = 1 level, in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: B̃_1 = 10.59 − 0.30 × (1 + 1/2) = 10.59 − 0.45 = 10.14 cm^−1. It is smaller than B̃_0 = 10.59 − 0.15 = 10.44 cm^−1, because the bond is longer on average in v = 1.

prompt: B̃ ∝ 1/R^2, where R is the bond length. For HCl, the average bond length in v = 1 is about 1.5% longer than in v = 0, so R_1 = 1.015R_0. What is the ratio B̃_1/B̃_0? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: B̃_1/B̃_0 = (R_0/R_1)^2 = 1/1.015^2 = 1/1.030 = 0.971. A bond 1.5% longer on average lowers B̃ by about 3%, as in B̃_1 = 10.14 cm^−1 against B̃_0 = 10.44 cm^−1.

prompt: With the vibration–rotation interaction, Ẽ_(v, J) = ν̃(v + 1/2) + B̃_v J(J + 1), so the J = 3 level lies 12B̃_v above the J = 0 level of the same v. For HCl, B̃_0 = 10.44 cm^−1 and B̃_1 = 10.14 cm^−1. How much smaller is this 12B̃_v in v = 1 than in v = 0, in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: J(J + 1) = 3 × 4 = 12. In v = 0: 12 × 10.44 = 125.28 cm^−1; in v = 1: 12 × 10.14 = 121.68 cm^−1. The difference is 12 × (10.44 − 10.14) = 12 × 0.30 = 3.6 cm^−1: the rotational ladder of v = 1 is slightly squeezed.

prompt: Once B̃ depends on v, which rotational constants are needed to predict the line positions of the v = 0 → 1 band?

choices.text: Both B̃_0 and B̃_1
Only B̃_0, of the lower level
choices.why: Each line ends on a v = 1 level, whose rotational energy uses B̃_1, so B̃_1 is needed as well as B̃_0.

choices.text: Only B̃_1, of the upper level
choices.why: Each line starts from a v = 0 level, whose rotational energy uses B̃_0. Only R(0), which starts from J = 0, has no B̃_0 in it.

choices.text: Only B̃_e, at the potential minimum
choices.why: B̃_e goes with R_e, the bottom of the well, but every level vibrates about it. The lines connect v = 0 and v = 1 levels, so they depend on B̃_0 and B̃_1.

explanation: Each line is Ẽ_(1, J′) − Ẽ_(0, J): the upper level's rotational energy uses B̃_1 and the lower level's uses B̃_0. That is why both constants appear in the formulas for ν̃_R and ν̃_P.

prompt: According to B̃_v = B̃_e − α̃_e(v + 1/2), how does B̃_0, the rotational constant of the lowest level, compare with B̃_e?

choices.text: Smaller, by α̃_e/2
Equal to it
choices.why: Putting v = 0 still leaves (0 + 1/2) = 1/2, so B̃_0 = B̃_e − α̃_e/2. Even the lowest level vibrates.

choices.text: Larger, by α̃_e/2
choices.why: The term α̃_e(v + 1/2) is subtracted, so B̃_0 is below B̃_e, not above it.

choices.text: Smaller, by α̃_e
choices.why: For v = 0 the factor (v + 1/2) is 1/2, not 1, so the drop is α̃_e/2. A drop of α̃_e is the step from one level to the next.

explanation: With v = 0, (v + 1/2) = 1/2, so B̃_0 = B̃_e − α̃_e/2. Even in its lowest level the molecule vibrates, so its average bond is a little longer than R_e and B̃_0 is a little below B̃_e.

prompt: Putting J = 0 into the R-branch formula gives ν̃_R = ν̃ + 2B̃_1. Why does only B̃_1 appear in the position of the R(0) line?

choices.text: Its lower level, J = 0, has no rotational energy
B̃_0 is zero for every molecule
choices.why: B̃_0 is not zero; for HCl it is over 10 cm^−1. It drops out because the lower level has J = 0, and B̃_0 × J(J + 1) = 0 there.

choices.text: B̃_1 and B̃_0 are always equal
choices.why: B̃_1 is smaller than B̃_0. B̃_0 drops out of R(0) because the starting level, J = 0, has no rotational energy.

choices.text: The R branch involves only the v = 1 vibrational level
choices.why: Every R line connects v = 0 to v = 1. For R(0), the v = 0 level has J = 0, so its rotational energy is zero.

explanation: R(0) goes from (v = 0, J = 0) to (v = 1, J = 1). The lower level's rotational energy B̃_0 × J(J + 1) is zero for J = 0, so only the upper level's rotational energy, B̃_1 × 1 × 2 = 2B̃_1, is added to ν̃.

prompt: Subtracting ν̃ from the R-branch formula gives ν̃_R − ν̃ = 2B̃_1 + (3B̃_1 − B̃_0)J + (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2. With B̃_0 = 10.44 cm^−1 and B̃_1 = 10.14 cm^−1, how far above ν̃ is the R(1) line (J = 1), in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)

In ν̃_R = ν̃ + 2B̃_1 + (3B̃_1 − B̃_0)J + (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2, the J^2 term has the coefficient (B̃_1 − B̃_0). For HCl, B̃_0 = 10.44 cm^−1 and B̃_1 = 10.14 cm^−1. What is (B̃_1 − B̃_0), in cm^−1, including its sign? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: B̃_1 − B̃_0 = 10.14 − 10.44 = −0.30 cm^−1. It is negative because B̃_1 < B̃_0, so the J^2 term pulls the lines toward lower wavenumber, more and more as J increases.

prompt: In ν̃_R = ν̃ + 2B̃_1 + (3B̃_1 − B̃_0)J + (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2, the coefficient (B̃_1 − B̃_0) is negative. What does the J^2 term do to the R-branch lines as J increases?

choices.text: Pulls higher-J lines down by more and more
Pushes higher-J lines up by more and more
choices.why: (B̃_1 − B̃_0) is negative, so the term subtracts, and it subtracts more at higher J. That squeezes the R lines together.

choices.text: Shifts every R line down by the same amount
choices.why: The term grows as J^2, so it lowers high-J lines much more than low-J lines. That is what squeezes the R lines together.

choices.text: Nothing, because it cancels the J term
choices.why: The J and J^2 terms don't cancel. The negative J^2 term pulls the higher-J lines down more and more, so the spacing shrinks.

explanation: Since B̃_1 < B̃_0, (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2 is negative and grows in size with J. Each R line is pulled down a bit more than the one before it, so the spacing between R lines decreases as J increases.

prompt: The same negative term, (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2, appears in both ν̃_R and ν̃_P. Why does it squeeze the R lines together but spread the P lines apart?

choices.text: P lines run downward, so the extra pull widens gaps
The J^2 term changes sign in the P-branch formula
choices.why: It is (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2 in both formulas, and B̃_1 < B̃_0, so it is negative in both. The difference is the direction the lines move as J grows.

choices.text: The P-branch formula contains only B̃_0, not B̃_1
choices.why: Both formulas contain B̃_0 and B̃_1. P lines move to lower wavenumber as J grows, so a growing downward pull widens their gaps.

choices.text: Centrifugal distortion acts only on the P-branch lines
choices.why: Centrifugal distortion affects both branches. Here the difference is that P lines move down as J grows, so the extra downward pull widens their gaps.

explanation: As J increases, R lines move up in wavenumber and P lines move down. A pull toward lower wavenumber that grows with J shortens the upward steps of the R branch but lengthens the downward steps of the P branch, so R spacings shrink and P spacings grow.

prompt: For the v = 0 → 1 band, the gap between the P-branch lines P(J) and P(J + 1) is 2B̃_0 + 2(B̃_0 − B̃_1)J. For HCl, B̃_0 = 10.44 cm^−1 and B̃_1 = 10.14 cm^−1. What is the gap between P(3) and P(4), in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 2 × 10.44 + 2 × (10.44 − 10.14) × 3 = 20.88 + 1.80 = 22.68 cm^−1. The gaps grow with J (21.5, 22.1, 22.7 and 23.3 cm^−1 for J = 1 to 4), which is why the P-branch lines spread apart.

prompt: Suppose B̃_1 were exactly equal to B̃_0. What would happen to the J^2 terms in ν̃_R and ν̃_P?

choices.text: They would vanish, leaving equally spaced lines
They would double, spreading all the lines apart
choices.why: With B̃_1 = B̃_0 the coefficient (B̃_1 − B̃_0) is zero, so the J^2 terms vanish rather than grow.

choices.text: They would become 2B̃J^2 in both branches
choices.why: The coefficient is the difference B̃_1 − B̃_0, not a sum, and it is zero when the two constants are equal.

choices.text: They would make both branches crowd together
choices.why: A zero coefficient has no effect at any J. Without the J^2 terms, and ignoring centrifugal distortion, the lines would be equally spaced.

explanation: With B̃_1 = B̃_0 = B̃, the coefficient (B̃_1 − B̃_0) is zero and the formulas become ν̃_R = ν̃ + 2B̃(J + 1) and ν̃_P = ν̃ − 2B̃J: lines 2B̃ apart, as in the simple model of the previous section. The unequal spacings come from B̃_1 differing from B̃_0.

prompt: Where in a vibration–rotation band is the effect of the (B̃_1 − B̃_0)J^2 terms most noticeable?

choices.text: At high J, far from the band center
At low J, right next to the band center
choices.why: The term grows as J^2, so it is smallest near the center, at low J, and largest far out in the branches.

choices.text: Equally at every J
choices.why: A term in J^2 is not the same for every line; it grows quickly as J increases.

choices.text: Only at the R(0) line
choices.why: At J = 0 the J^2 term is zero. Its effect grows as J^2, so it is largest at high J.

explanation: B̃_1 − B̃_0 is small, but it is multiplied by J^2, which grows quickly. So the departure from equal spacing is small near the band center and grows toward the far ends of the P and R branches.

prompt: In the HCl spectrum, the P(1) line is at 2865.1 cm^−1 and the R(0) line is at 2906.3 cm^−1. How wide is the gap between these two lines, in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 2906.3 − 2865.1 = 41.2 cm^−1. From the branch formulas, R(0) is 2B̃_1 above ν̃ and P(1) is 2B̃_0 below it, so the gap is 2B̃_1 + 2B̃_0 = 20.28 + 20.88 = 41.16 cm^−1, a little less than 4B̃_0 = 41.76 cm^−1 because B̃_1 < B̃_0.
